title: The hit-and-run cab
paradigm: Kahneman & Tversky (1972) cab problem; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) frequency format

probability.intro: A cab was involved in a hit-and-run accident at night. Two cab companies, Green and Blue, operate in the city. 85% of the cabs are Green and 15% are Blue. A witness identified the cab as Blue. The court tested the witness under the same conditions and found that the witness correctly identified each colour 80% of the time.
probability.question: What is the probability (0-100%) that the cab involved in the accident was Blue?

frequency.intro: A cab was involved in a hit-and-run accident at night. Out of every 100 cabs in the city, 85 are Green and 15 are Blue. A witness identified the cab as Blue. When tested, the witness correctly identified the colour of 80 out of every 100 cabs, and got the other 20 wrong.
frequency.question: Out of 100 accidents like this one where the witness says 'Blue', how many involved a Blue cab? Give your answer as a number from 0 to 100.

debrief: Of 100 cabs, 15 are Blue and the witness gets 12 of them right; 85 are Green and the witness wrongly calls 17 of them Blue. So when the witness says Blue, 12 of 29 cases (41%) are really Blue. Most people answer around 80% because they use the witness's reliability and ignore the base rate.
